# The name Yama and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Yama** ​opens onto the domain of death, justice, underworld, the Sanskrit tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post moves through that world room by room — the ‌name and its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, and its afterlife — before arriving at the digital temple that makes ‌the record addressable. The letters are plain; the evidence is not.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Yama
- **ASCII form:** yama
- **Meaning:** "The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the ​departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead."
- **Domain of influence:** Death, Justice, Underworld
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** यम (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Yama** (*yama*) — Death, the ​First Mortal, Judge of the Dead · The god who presides over the Pitṛs — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Death, Justice, ​Underworld". The name means "The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead.".

**Yama** is death’s king in the Indian traditions: ​the first man to die, who found the way to the fathers’ world and now rules it — and judges who may enter. With his noose and his two ​four-eyed dogs, he waits at the southern direction, the realm of the ancestors, and his account-book is the oldest audit in human literature.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari ​as **यम**. Etymologically it means "The god who presides over the Pitṛs (the departed fathers) and rules the spirits of the dead.".

The canonical spelling **Yama** matches the conventional ‌scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *yama* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one reviewed reference spelling, ​preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in ​Devanagari as **यम**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Yama*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Yama is written in Devanagari as यम
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and ‌consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name ​is **/ˈjʌmə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Yama).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ya-** — Palatal y as in “young”; the a is short and open.
- **-ma** — The name means “twin” — ​Yama is the twin of Yamī in the earliest tradition.
- **Yam-** — In compound names the stem surfaces as yam- — the river Yamunā preserves his twin sister’s name.

​For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “YUM-uh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Avestan** — Yima
- **Vedic** — Yamī (his twin sister)
- **Buddhist** — Yama/Enma

The ​lord of the dead was the first mortal — the one who found the path and guards it ever since.

## Mythology

Yama’s mythology moves from Vedic pathfinder to epic judge ​to Purāṇic king of hells. He begins as the twin who chose to die — the first of the race to walk the path — and becomes the stern ‌accountant whose city the dead enter by the southern gate. Buddhism and the epics gave him his tortures and his buffalo; the Veda kept his dignity.

### The Twin Dialogue ​(Rigveda 10.10)

The oldest Yama-text is a dialogue: Yama and his twin Yamī, the first two beings, and Yamī’s love for her brother. Yama refuses — ‘the immortals watch’ ‌— and the hymn becomes the charter of exogamy and of the incest-taboo itself, argued between the world’s first twins in the world’s first debate.

### The Path of the ​Fathers (Rigveda 10.14)

The funeral hymn sends the dead king along the path Yama blazed, past the two dogs and the waters, to the feast of the fathers where ‌Yama waits with Varuṇa. ‘Leave the sin here, keep the glory’ — the formula of every Vedic funeral, spoken to the first traveller’s successor.

### The King Under the Earth ​(Mahābhārata)

In the epic’s underworld-book, Yama rules below with his city Saṃyamanī, his account read by Citragupta, his noose and his buffalo — the god of justice who once ‌disguised himself as a crab to test a king. The epic makes him dreaded and fair: the judge who cannot be bribed because he already owns everything.

### The Lord of ​the Narakas (Purāṇic Hell)

The Purāṇas enumerate eighty-four hells under Yama’s administration, each a precise torment for a precise sin — the liar’s tongue, the thief’s hands. Yet the ‌same texts insist his justice is karma’s arithmetic, not malice: even the tortures are purification, and release comes in time.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Yama concentrates ​in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The First Mortal** — He died before anyone — the twin who found the path ​to the fathers and became its king.
- **The Noose** — His pāśa, the noose, finds every soul at its hour; none outrun it, though all may beg.
- **The Two ‌Dogs** — Śyāma and Śabala, four-eyed, follow his road and report the dead; they guard the way.
- **Judge of the Deeds** — In the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas he reads ‌the record of every soul — the karma, weighed without scales.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Yama survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued ‌below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

No Yama temples in the Vedic sphere — the ancestor-cult needed ​no image. But his buffalo and noose carved into the doorposts of death-temples across Nepal and Bali, and the Enma iconography of Japanese temples from Kamakura onward, mark the reach ​of his cult east.

## Realm & Domain

**Yama** is death’s king in the Indian traditions: the first man to die, who found the way to the fathers’ world and ‌now rules it — and judges who may enter. With his noose and his two four-eyed dogs, he waits at the southern direction, the realm of the ancestors, and ​his account-book is the oldest audit in human literature.

### The First Mortal

He died before anyone — the twin who found the path to the fathers and became its ​king.

### The Noose

His pāśa, the noose, finds every soul at its hour; none outrun it, though all may beg.

### The Two Dogs

Śyāma and Śabala, four-eyed, follow his ‌road and report the dead; they guard the way.

### Judge of the Deeds

In the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas he reads the record of every soul — the karma, weighed ​without scales.

## Across Cultures

The Avestan Yima, king of the golden age who kept death from his realm, is Yama’s Iranian twin — the same name, opposite function: where ​Yima postponed death, Yama administers it. Buddhism made Yama a dharmapāla, converted in the end by the Buddha’s teaching, and carried him east as Enma in Japan, where he ‌still judges with his mirror and staff.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[hades|Hádēs]] (underworld / death), [[anubis|ꜣnpw]] (underworld / death), [[cerberus|Kérberos]] (underworld / death), [[ereshkigal|Ereškigal]] (underworld / ​death), [[forseti|Forseti]] (justice / law / truth), and [[garmr|Garmr]] (underworld / death).

## Cultural Legacy

Yama is the ancestor of every Asian judge-of-the-dead: Enma-ō in Japan, Yŏmna in Korea, Yanluo ‌in China — a continuous iconography from the Veda to manga. The word ‘Yamī’ survives in the river Yamunā; and the maxim ‘even Yama’s writ runs by karma’ structures ​the moral imagination of half the world’s population.

## A Meditation

Yama: the twin’s name, the first word of mortality. Restored plainly, ​it reads as what it is — a name without ornament for the fact without ornament. Every other god in this lexicon borrows grandeur; Yama IS, which is why ‌his name is the shortest sentence in Sanskrit.
